blocks.text: And, so that the Argo may be believed to have been a very swift ship, the poets describe it as quick ὅσον πελειάδος [hoson peleiados], like a dove. And they invent the story that a dove was sent by the Argonauts between the Symplegades, and that when it had got through, they concluded from this that the Argo too would get through, as Eustathius teaches on Odyssey μ´. The Arabs and Hebrews agree with this. Thus Damir, after teaching that الشهرمان والشاهين [al-shahramān wa-l-shāhīn], the saharman and the sahin, species of hawk, are most hostile to the dove, says: وهو اطير منهما ومن ساير الطير كلها [wa-huwa aṭyar minhumā wa-min sāyir al-ṭayr kullihā] And it surpasses them in flight, and all birds whatsoever. And on the passage of the Psalm that we have cited, R. Simon, R. Iodan, R. Jonah, and R. Kimchi, to the question why David prefers the wings of the dove to the wings of other birds, answer thus: כל העופות בשעה שיגעים הם נסים על גבי הסלע או על גבי האילן ונתפסין אבל יונה בשעה שיגעה היא קובצת אחת מאגפיה ופורחת באחת והיא נצולת ואינה נתפסת, All other birds, when they are tired from flying, flee onto a rock or onto a tree, and are caught; but the dove, when it is tired, folds one of its wings and flies with the other, and so escapes and is not caught. And Aben Ezra: והזכיר יונה [col. 15] שהיא עם בני אדם ועמה ישגרו המלכים ספריהם, He mentions the dove because it lives with men, and kings send letters by it. Indeed, in the twelfth century after Christ, when Aben Ezra wrote, this was much practised. Paulus Aemilius, On the Deeds of the Franks, book 4, where he speaks of the governor of Hasarchum, a town of Syria: His envoys (sent to Baldwin to beg for help) tied a letter to the tail of a dove which they had brought with them from home when they set out on their embassy, and sent it back as agreed. Thus informed, the governor defended himself excellently [II, 543]. And where he speaks of Jerusalem besieged by the Christians: It happened that a dove flying over the camp of the Latins, descending as a hawk pressed upon it, was caught by our men. Under its wings was found a letter written in Arabic, both in words and in letters. And in book 5: While they were encamped before the walls (of Tyre), some authors say that a dove flew up. When our men, taught by experience, recognized it as a letter-carrier, so great a shout was raised by the land and naval forces of the Latins that the bird, as if driven by a whirlwind of the disturbed air, fell to the ground. The letter taken from it, written in barbarian characters to the Tyrians, said that help would soon come, that they should be of good courage and endure the siege a few days. Our men, on the other hand, had another letter written in the hand and language of those barbarians whom they held in their power etc. and sent the bird back with the forged and deceitful letter, telling the besieged to take counsel for themselves according to their present need, etc. that no hope of help near at hand could be held out, etc. The Tyrians yielded to the trick. Marmol, in his Africa, book 2, chapter 31, refers this to the year 1123. On the same matter see Jacques de Vitry, Histor. Orient. book 1; Arnold of Lübeck in the History of the Slavs; Vincent in the Doctrinale book 16, ch. 154; and Wildebrand of Oldenburg in the Itinerarium Hierosolymitanum, where he wrongly ascribes to the people of Tripoli what others attribute to the Tyrians. But older histories too offer us examples of the same art. For, to pass over fables, such as what the Samaritans write in chapter 20 of their spurious book of Joshua, that after defeating the five kings he informed Eleazar of this victory by a letter tied to the wings of birds, and in chapter 34 that he sent a letter to Nebichus by the service of a dove; and what we read in Aelian, History, book 6, chapter 7, that Mares, king of Egypt, used a crow to carry letters wherever he wished: to pass over these, I say, since they are plainly fabulous, why should we not believe what is found in Aelian's Varia, book 9, chapter 2, that Taurosthenes, the Ὀλυμπιονίκην [Olympionikēn], announced his victory to his father in Aegina from Olympia on the same day by a dove as messenger? They say, namely, περιστερὰν τὸν Ταυροσθένην ἐπάγεσθαι ἀπολιποῦσαν τοὺς ἑαυτῆς νεοσσοὺς ὑγροὺς ἔτι, καὶ ἀπτῆνας, νικήσαντα, καὶ ἀφεῖναι τὴν πελειάδα, προσάψαντα πορφύραν αὐτῇ· τὴν δὲ ἐπειγομένην πρὸς τοὺς νεοττοὺς, ἀπαυθημερῆσαι ἐκ Πίσσης εἰς Αἴγιναν· [peristeran ton Taurosthenēn epagesthai apolipousan tous heautēs neossous hygrous eti, kai aptēnas, nikēsanta, kai apheinai tēn peleiada, prosapsanta porphyran autē; tēn de epeigomenēn pros tous neottous, apauthēmerēsai ek Pissēs eis Aiginan] that Taurosthenes took with him a dove taken away from its chicks, still tender and unfledged; and when he had won, he sent it back with a piece of purple tied to it, and it, hastening with all speed to its chicks, flew on the same day from Pisa to Aegina. Pliny and Frontinus report that something similar happened at the siege of Mutina, although they hardly agree with each other. For the latter, in book 3 of the Stratagems, writes that Hirtius sent letters, tied with a bristle to a dove's neck, to Decimus Brutus, besieged in Mutina by Antony; the former, in book 10, chapter 37, says that doves were messengers in great affairs, with letters attached to their feet, at the siege of Mutina, when D. Brutus sent them to the consuls' camp. But in the same siege [II, 544] the same Brutus could have both received and sent back letters by the service of doves.
